transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-10-05
Time: 14:30 - 15:32 UTC
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Elena (Redwood SE), Priya (Redwood Solutions), Ravi (Mimir ML Lead), Dana (Mimir SRE), Owen (Mimir Applied ML)

Summary:
Broad technical deep dive on mixed-precision runtime behavior (INT8 / FP8 / AWQ / GPTQ), with a focus on a reproducible accuracy regression Mimir is seeing in long-context retrieval scenarios when KV cache is heavily utilized and VPC network tail-latency occurs. SE walked through profiling plan and suggested fallbacks and hotfixes. Agreed next steps: run targeted micro-benchmarks, share prompts, run on-prem pilot.

Topics covered:
- Reproducible regression pattern when mixing AWQ + dynamic KV cache replay
- Interaction between quantized kernel selection and KV cache prefetch/warmup
- Batching/coalescing heuristics under noisy VPC egress
- Fallback ordering for precision cascade and model variant routing
- Security/operations constraints for Mimir's air-gapped staging cluster

Action items (short):
- Elena: share perf traces and modified runner config
- Ravi: share failing prompts and dataset slice
- Jordan: update pilot pricing and security checklist

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan: okay, uh thanks everyone for joining, we'll do a deep dive, we're expecting about an hour, apologies if we run over, can you each quick intro?
[00:12] Ravi: yeah sure, I'm Ravi, lead for the platform, we've been running your hosted API for prototypes but hitting this weird accuracy drop in long-retrieval, trying to understand if it's an inference bug or quantization artifact.
[00:25] Dana: Dana, SRE, I'll focus on net and infra, we run in a VPC with egress NAT, possible tail lat spikes.
[00:33] Owen: Owen, applied ML, I built the retrieval+rerank stack, we see divergence after ~1.2k tokens when KV cache is warm.
[00:40] Elena: Elena from Redwood, I'll take the technical lead on profiling and the tracer outputs, hi all.
[00:46] Jordan: quick agenda, reproduce pattern, review traces, propose fixes: precision fallback, KV warmup tuning, batching tweaks, and an on-prem plan.

[02:05] Elena: okay, show me a high-level reproduction first: what's the model and quant setup?
[02:11] Owen: we're using an open 30B transformer, converted with AWQ 4-bit per-channel, but then we've layered a runtime INT8 bias-correct path for the attention matmul to accelerate generation. We also tried GPTQ baseline earlier, GPTQ didn't regress but was 2.5x slower on our infra.
[02:35] Elena: interesting — so AWQ combined with an INT8 runtime path; that mixing can hit numeric path differences. Important detail: are you using per-layer fallback?
[02:44] Owen: we don't currently do layer-wise fallback. It's an all-or-nothing config because our older runner didn't expose layer granularity.

[03:15] Dana: and the failing cases correlate with spikes in network latency; we see NAT gateway tail spikes to other regions, which seems to stall KV prefetches briefly.
[03:26] Elena: stalling KV prefetch is key. If the KV is stale or missing and batching coalescer holds requests, the runtime may pick a lower-precision kernel because token sequences appear shorter — uhm, or we saw scheduling pick the AWQ path less often, leading to mismatch.

[04:05] Jordan: can you describe the divergence? is it lexical degradation or hallucination?
[04:12] Owen: mostly hallucination in rerank — model drifts and starts inventing facts not present in context, confidence remains high. It's subtle but reproduction is consistent across seeds.
[04:25] Elena: that smells like quant noise accumulating in attention where KV reuse amplifies errors. If AWQ reduces head precision in key/value projectors, small errors can compound when keys are reused many times in long-context.

[05:00] Ravi: we ran an A/B where we disabled KV caching entirely and the drift went away, but latency doubled which we can't accept.
[05:11] Elena: right, disabling cache removes the amplification but loses perf. So aim is: keep KV cache but reduce quantization sensitivity or add selective fallbacks without losing all throughput.

[06:00] Elena: first diagnostic: we need a micro-benchmark that replays the exact token timing including VPC egress spikes, not just sequence content. The tracer needs to mark KV hits/misses and kernel-choice per layer per token.
[06:25] Dana: we can simulate NAT tail spikes in staging and run the replay, we'll share packet captures.

[07:10] Elena: good. On the runtime side, three levers: (1) precision cascade (per-layer fallbacks from AWQ -> INT8 -> FP16), (2) KV warmup policies (sticky KV warmup threshold, prefetch on first n prompts), (3) batching preemption (do not coalesce into large batches when KV cache hit rate drops).

[08:00] Owen: about the precision cascade, how expensive is dynamic fallback? We worry about jitter.
[08:10] Elena: there's overhead but it's mostly per-layer kernel switch cost — on our tests it's 5-12% latency increase when a small fraction of tokens trigger fallback. The gain is correctness: prevents drift.

[09:00] Jordan: and can fallback be prioritized for attention layers only?
[09:06] Elena: yes — we recommend first-tier fallback only on Q/K/V projectors and attention matmul; keeping FFN in AWQ yields most perf. The runtime supports per-op policy since last quarter.

[10:05] Ravi: what about mixed INT8 path you mentioned — could that be causing double quantization?
[10:12] Elena: exactly — converting AWQ-quantized weights into an INT8 execution kernel without dequant/debias steps can lead to mismatched scale assumptions. We saw one customer where combining AWQ encoding with an INT8 fast GEMM introduced bias in attention scores.

[11:00] Owen: is it better to re-run a pure GPTQ for us? We tried GPTQ earlier but perf was worse.
[11:08] Elena: GPTQ tends to preserve accuracy better because it's a globally optimized quantization, but it can be slower or larger. A middle-ground: use AWQ for FFN and GPTQ or FP16 for attention. That is, mixed-quant profile per sub-block.

[12:00] Dana: operationally we run in a VPC on dedicated hosts for staging, will the private deployment keep behavior identical?
[12:10] Elena: on Private deployments behavior is identical for the runtime; however network jitter in VPC still matters. Private on-prem avoids NAT gateway spikes but you can still see cross-subnet egress delays. We instrumented the KV warmup to be tolerant to 100-200ms occasional delays but when delays exceed that, warmup misses occur.

[13:05] Owen: can we detect warmup misses and trigger immediate prefetch?
[13:10] Elena: yes — runtime emits a KV miss rate metric and we can attach a policy: if miss_rate > 5% for 10s, force immediate prefetch of last N prompts and prioritize key fill. That buys accuracy at the cost of a small burst.

[14:00] Jordan: what about batching behavior — we suspect coalescing masks the timing of tokens and changes kernel selection.
[14:10] Elena: right. The coalescer tries to batch sequences by length and inferred latency window. Under variable network latency batching can accidentally fuse tokens across different KV states; we added a guard: don't conflate requests with KV stale indicator set.

[15:00] Ravi: that sounds promising. How invasive is that change for our on-prem runner?
[15:05] Elena: it's a config flip — coalescer already exposes a KV-aware mode in our bin since v1.9.0; enabling it has negligible overhead. We'll share the exact flag.

[16:00] Owen: we want to understand exact numeric delta: how to measure whether fallback prevents hallucination without a human in loop?
[16:08] Elena: create an automated eval that runs the prompt suite, computes an F1/pass-fail on factual checks or checks reranker ranking stability; track drift metric across token windows. We'll provide a sample eval harness.

[17:00] Elena: I'll outline a two-phase plan: (A) reproduce locally with staging using simulated NAT spikes and our micro-benchmark, (B) run a controlled canary on dedicated nodes with per-layer fallback enabled for attention, KV-aware batching enabled, and AWQ only for FFN. Observe accuracy and latency impact.

[18:30] Owen: for the canary, what's the recommended traffic split?
[18:35] Elena: start 5% with traffic ramp to 25% over 24h if no regressions. Also pin a stable model variant as fallback route.

[19:20] Dana: security note: our staging is air-gapped, we need the private installer and signed artifacts. What's the cadence on new runtime builds?
[19:28] Jordan: we have quarterly private builds, but for customers in pilot we can run an emergency build; we'll need SSO and a signed NDA first.

[20:00] Ravi: any known incompatibilities with HSM/KMS workflows? we manage keys with AWS KMS; private installs use customer HSM for model keys.
[20:09] Elena: runtime key ops are independent — quant profiles and kernel binaries don't carry secrets. HSM for model signing is supported; we'll share the integration guide.

[21:15] Owen: one more question — how do we mitigate the latency hit when a rollback to FP16 happens mid-stream for a small fraction of tokens? customers worry about tail latency spikes.
[21:26] Elena: good question. We recommend two mechanisms: (1) pre-reserve a small pool of FP16 fast path workers to absorb fallback bursts, (2) use a token-level pacing policy: if fallback triggers, slow-batch following tokens slightly to amortize kernel switch cost — it's a few ms per token but reduces percentile spikes.

[22:30] Jordan: Elena, can you quantify expected p95 delta for our 30B workload if we enable attention-only fallback?
[22:38] Elena: on our infra p95 increases by about 8-15% depending on fallback frequency. If fallback is rare (<2% tokens) p95 hit is ~6-8%. If frequent (10% tokens) could reach 20%+. We'll include exact numbers from our bench.

[24:00] Ravi: what's the instrumentation we should send you? traces, kernel decisions, KV hit timeline, and net pcap?
[24:08] Elena: yes exactly — we need per-token trace: timestamp, token_id (anonymized), kv_hit boolean, kernel_choice, layer, latency_ms. Plus system metrics and pcap for the NAT tail window.

[25:00] Owen: we'll anonymize token ids; can you accept that?
[25:03] Elena: absolutely–we only need stable ids to correlate.

[26:00] Jordan: there's been talk about AWQ variants that include a small calibration table to reduce attention bias. Is that something enough to fix this without fallbacks?
[26:12] Elena: calibration tables help, but they add memory; they reduce bias in certain ops but don't eliminate accumulation over long KV reuse. They are a good supplement to fallback+warmup policies.

[27:15] Dana: if we move to dedicated private nodes, does the runtime still choose the same kernels? any hardware-specific tuning?
[27:22] Elena: yes it selects kernels per device; for dedicated GPUs we can bake a tuned profile. There's a small perf variance across GPU models, but kernel selection is deterministic given the profile.

[28:30] Owen: we're worried about regression after software updates. Any advice?
[28:36] Elena: recommend pinned model+runtime combo and a regression suite that runs post-deploy. Redwood Console can automatically run smoke evals on rollout.

[30:00] Elena: quick demo — (screen share) here's a trace where we forced a 250ms NAT spike mid-prompt; notice at token ~1120 the KV miss rate jumps and the kernel-path flips, after 8 tokens the outputs diverged.
[30:45] Owen: I see the divergence; the attention logits look shifted.
[31:10] Elena: imagine that compounding over many layers. It's small per-step difference but accumulates.

[32:00] Ravi: if we do the plan, how long until pilot? timeline?
[32:07] Jordan: if we get traces and prompts this week, SE will run local repros and ship a canary build by Oct 14; then you can run on-prem the week-of Oct 18.

[33:00] Owen: about cost — if we enable FP16 fallback more often, does pricing change for dedicated nodes?
[33:06] Jordan: fallback itself doesn't change billing model; cost impact is on GPU utilization — higher p95 and lower throughput effectively increases unit cost. For Dedicated we can size burst nodes accordingly and provide cost projection.

[34:00] Dana: what's the rollback plan if canary shows regression?
[34:05] Elena: immediate route-level rollback to previous model variant plus traffic cutover to hosted fallback. We'll also capture traces for triage.

[35:20] Owen: any quick wins we can apply now?
[35:25] Elena: three quick wins: (1) enable KV-aware coalescing flag, (2) bump KV warmup threshold to prefetch N=5 instead of N=1, (3) apply attention-only FP16 fallback with a low sampling percent (1%) to evaluate impact. These are config changes, minimal deploy.

[36:00] Ravi: good. We'll prioritize flags to staging.

[37:00] Jordan: let's talk about observability and alerts—what thresholds to set?
[37:06] Elena: set KV miss rate alert at 3% sustained, regression alert if drift metric deviates more than X sigma from baseline, and p95 latency increase >15% for 10m.

[38:00] Owen: are there any corner cases where fallback makes outputs worse?
[38:05] Elena: rare but possible: switching precision mid-sequence can create discontinuity if not handled with smoothing — the runtime adds a micro-debias step on switching now, but very aggressive fallback toggling could produce jitter. Hence the pacing policy.

[39:00] Dana: from security/compliance side, anything new?
[39:05] Jordan: nothing major. We will share the signed SBOM, audit log options and the offline installer.

[40:00] Elena: final technical note — for extremely long contexts (>4k) consider a mixed caching strategy: hot-key sticky cache for last K tokens plus compressed KV for distant context with lower-precision kernels; that reduces warmup sensitivity.

[41:00] Owen: that might map well to our retrieval architecture.

[42:00] Jordan: quick recap of decisions and owners then close?
[42:08] Elena: reproduce with micro-bench (Elena), share traces (Mimir), enable flags in staging (Mimir + Redwood), run canary (Redwood + Mimir).

[43:00] Ravi: agreed, we'll get traces in by Friday.

[44:00] Jordan: any final questions?
[44:03] Owen: none from me.
[44:10] Dana: nope.
[45:00] Jordan: great, I'll send notes and the config diffs and schedule follow-up for Oct 14 canary review. Thanks all.

[61:30] Meeting end
